findings.title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed
findings.body: Processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which yields `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (= `multiprocessing.context.Process`), so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` evaluates to False. In `_ensure_processes_alive` this means `process.kill()` is never called when a process is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`). Before this PR `kill()` was invoked unconditionally. Consequence: a hung-but-alive flusher is leaked and a second process is started for the same shards; if the old one resumes, two flushers concurrently run `flush_segments`/`done_flush_segments` on the same Redis shards, which can produce duplicate segments to buffered-segments and double the Redis load. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`) instead. The same wrong check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is also never called there.

findings.title: join() stops terminating remaining processes once the deadline passes
findings.body: In `join()`, when the deadline has elapsed the loop does `break`, which skips `process.terminate()` for every process not yet visited. Previously the single process was always terminated after the wait. With several flusher processes, any that haven't exited by the join timeout are left running (only the `stopped` flag is set, which a hung process ignores). The `break` should be removed so each remaining process still gets `terminate()` called (the inner `while` already respects the deadline).

findings.title: Redis memory info is fetched once per flusher process instead of once per cluster
findings.body: `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` returns memory usage for every node of the Redis cluster, not just the buffer's shards. `submit()` now calls it for each per-process `SpansBuffer` and sums the results. With N flusher processes this issues N times as many `INFO memory` calls to every Redis node on every submit, and `used`/`available` are each over-counted N times (the ratio happens to survive, but the values are wrong if anyone logs/reports them). Since the check is cluster-wide, it should run once (e.g. on a single buffer) rather than per process.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag names: "shard" vs "shards"
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `{"shard": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` on the same code path uses `{"shards": shard_tag}`, and `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` uses `shard` with a single int. The same comma-joined value is emitted under two different tag keys, which makes dashboards/queries inconsistent. Pick one tag name.

findings.title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but default is a single process
findings.body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but `max_processes` caps the count, and the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1, so in the default deployment all shards share one process. The docstring should describe the `max_processes` parameter and the shard-to-process distribution instead.

findings.title: No test covers the real multiprocess path or process restart
findings.body: Both new/updated tests pass `produce_to_pipe`, which forces the `threading.Thread` code path. The actual `mp_context.Process` branch (pickling the per-shard buffer, `run_with_initialized_sentry`, `is_alive`/`kill`/`terminate` handling in `_ensure_processes_alive` and `join`) is never exercised, which is exactly where the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` bug lives. `test_flusher_processes_limit` also only asserts the total shard count; it does not check that shards are disjoint across processes or that a dead process is recreated for the same shards. Adding a test that spawns at least one real process (or a restart test with a thread that exits early) would catch regressions here.
